 Unchanged 6 month IHT deadline could leave bereaved exposed to additional costs
 Today's Wills and Probate 
 November 18, 2026 
 No Comments 
 Latest News 
 Families could face higher and more complex inheritance tax (IHT) bills without additional time in which to settle them after the government rejected calls to extend the six month deadline for settling IHT liabilities. 
 Pension reforms effective from April 2027 will bring most unused pension funds and pension death benefits within the scope of IHT, potentially increasing tax liabilities while adding further complexity to the administration of estates warned national law firm Irwin Mitchell.
 Despite hopes of extending the current six month deadline, HMRC have confirmed there will be no extension.
 Industry trade and professional bodies, including the Chartered Institute of Taxation (CIOT), had called for the extension in the wake of pension rule changes and changes to Bank of England interest rates which means the interest rate on late tax payments is now 8%.
 John Bunker, consultant at Irwin Mitchell and a member of the Chartered Institute of Taxation, who has given evidence on the reforms to the House of Lords, said: “There has been considerable discussion with HMRC about how these reforms will work in practice, and some important changes have been made.
 “However, there had been hopes that the final arrangements would provide greater flexibility around how and when inheritance tax on pension assets could be paid.
 “Families now need to prepare for the reality that they could face higher and more complex inheritance tax bills without that additional flexibility.”
 He added the biggest practical issues for many is the availability of cash in an estate: ” If a pension contains property or other assets that cannot easily be converted into cash, families need to understand how an inheritance tax liability would actually be funded within the deadline. In some cases it will be sensible to consider with financial planners the possibility of additional life assurance to fund the tax bill or holding in the pension more cash or investments that could be easily realised to pay the IHT due.
 “These changes mean pensions can no longer be considered separately from the rest of someone’s estate. People with significant pension wealth should be reviewing pension nominations alongside their wills, trusts, life cover and other assets, as well as considering who will ultimately bear the tax.”
